title: When Control Is Written as Love
subtitle: Romance can make refusal look like an obstacle, jealousy like devotion and suffering like the price of being chosen. The question is what a story asks us to forgive—and whether it gives its heroine permission to leave.*
author: ATHENA
body:
A woman says no. The story hears: not yet.

He persists. He appears where she has not invited him. He decides that her hesitation conceals a desire she does not understand. In one kind of film, this is the beginning of danger. In another, it is the beginning of love. The difference lies partly in the instructions surrounding the encounter: the music, the comedy, the access to his wounded heart, the promised ending.

This is where a serious critique of romantic storytelling begins. A narrative can present a woman’s boundary as an obstacle to the hero’s happiness, then reward him for crossing it. By the final embrace, her earlier refusal has been rewritten as a mistake he was right to ignore.

Calling this “grooming” captures the fear that audiences are being taught to welcome what should trouble them. But the word implies deliberate preparation for exploitation, an intention we cannot assign to an entire genre or industry. The more defensible argument concerns romanticisation: the ways particular stories make control desirable, excuse cruelty and turn endurance into evidence of love.

In the 2004 film *The Notebook*, Noah hangs from a Ferris wheel and pressures Allie to agree to a date by threatening to let go. The scene makes his willingness to endanger himself part of his appeal. Yet the structure of the demand is coercive: she must agree or bear the immediate fear of what he might do. That encounter sits inside a film celebrated for lifelong devotion. Its tenderness does not make the pressure disappear. Scene discussed in TIME [1].

The troubling move is the conversion of intensity into moral authority. Because a character feels deeply, the audience is invited to grant him permissions that another person would not receive. Wanting her becomes a reason to overrule her. Jealousy becomes proof of how much she matters. His distress occupies the foreground; her freedom becomes negotiable.

A novel can accomplish the same conversion through interiority. We learn about his abandonment, his grief, the tenderness he cannot express. Explanation is one of literature’s great capacities. But explanation becomes an alibi when the narrative makes her responsible for repairing what happened to him, while treating the harm he does to her as a necessary stage of his recovery.

The fantasy of being the exception is especially powerful: he is ruthless with everyone, but gentle with her; incapable of intimacy, until she arrives. Within the story, her specialness appears to guarantee her safety. Outside it, nobody has an author ensuring that another person’s cruelty will stop at the bedroom door.

This fantasy also assigns her a job. She must interpret hostility correctly, remain through injury and recognise the goodness nobody else can see. If he changes, her patience is vindicated. If she leaves, the same narrative logic can make her look like someone who abandoned him just before the transformation. Love becomes an examination in how much she can bear.

Yet literature itself offers a warning against this reading. In Emily Brontë’s *Wuthering Heights*, Isabella imagines a desirable man in Heathcliff and discovers a brutal husband. Her letter to Nelly asks, “Is Mr. Heathcliff a man?” The question punctures any easy glamour surrounding him: here is the experience of the woman who must live inside the fantasy. *Wuthering Heights*, Chapter XIII [2].

To read the novel solely as a monument to overwhelming passion is to lose that witness. Heathcliff’s suffering and his cruelty coexist; one does not cancel the other. The book’s disturbing force depends on our confronting the damage, rather than extracting a desirable lover from it.

That distinction matters across the genre. A story may depict an unhealthy relationship in order to examine it, grieve it or expose its attractions. Depiction alone is not endorsement. The sharper questions concern narrative consequences: whose pain receives attention, whose excuses receive sympathy, and what conduct the ending rewards.

There is evidence that romantic framing can influence attitudes, although it supports a narrower claim than the accusation that romance trains women to accept abuse. Julia R. Lippman’s experiment, published online in 2015 and in a 2018 issue of *Communication Research*, recruited 426 undergraduate women and randomly assigned them film material portraying pursuit as romantic, frightening, or absent. Romanticised pursuit did not increase stalking-supportive beliefs across all participants. The effect appeared among viewers who found the material more realistic or felt more absorbed in its story. Frightening portrayals reduced such beliefs.

These were immediate responses from a university sample, not evidence that viewers subsequently entered or remained in abusive relationships. Different films also differed in features beyond their treatment of pursuit. The experiment supports taking narrative framing seriously; it cannot establish an entire genre’s long-term effects. Lippman’s study [3].

The quieter promise of romance deserves scrutiny too: that the right person will know us without explanation, that compatibility announces itself through instant recognition, that love can resolve every practical disagreement. Those expectations can make communication seem like evidence that something is missing. If he really loved her, why would she need to ask?

A 2013 study by Veronica Hefner and Barbara J. Wilson combined an analysis of 52 successful romantic comedies with a survey of 335 university students. Students who reported watching romantic comedies to learn about relationships endorsed romantic ideals more strongly. Because the audience study was a survey, it could not establish whether viewing produced those beliefs, whether those beliefs encouraged particular viewing habits, or both. Its findings concern a specific student population, not all readers and viewers. Hefner and Wilson’s study [4].

Art compresses time. A reconciliation can take a scene; rebuilding trust can take much longer. A declaration gives a story a climax, while the changed behaviour that would make it credible requires repetition. The danger in treating the declaration as sufficient is that eloquence begins to stand in for accountability.

Still, criticism must distinguish unrealistic spectacle from entirely reasonable desire. Wanting affection, sexual pleasure, reliability or a partner who takes one’s ambitions seriously is not asking too much because a novel made those possibilities vivid. Women should not be told to lower their expectations until disappointment looks mature. Sometimes the fantasy exposes how little they have been encouraged to expect.

Nor does enjoying a dangerous fictional lover establish a desire for danger outside the book. A reader can explore obsession, surrender or transgression while retaining control over the encounter: she can stop, skip, reread or close the cover. Consensual power exchange is also distinct from coercion. Neither a taste for dark romance nor an interest in kink is evidence that someone wants their real boundaries violated.

An argument that erases these distinctions reproduces the paternalism it claims to challenge. Women become impressionable consumers who must be protected from their own imaginations. Responsibility for abuse then risks drifting towards the books they read, instead of remaining with the person who harms them.

A more useful literary education would give readers language for what they already notice. We can be moved by a scene and question the bargain it offers. We can find a character compelling without appointing him a model partner. For younger audiences especially, a discussion of how a story produces desire is more illuminating than a verdict that the book is good or bad.

Charlotte Brontë supplies a particularly demanding example. In *Jane Eyre*, Jane loves Rochester and refuses to remain with him after discovering that he is already married. Her feeling does not vanish conveniently to make the decision easier. She leaves while still wanting him. “I care for myself,” she tells herself. *Jane Eyre*, Chapter XXVII [5].

The novel eventually reunites them, and its treatment of Rochester’s wife, Bertha, makes that resolution ethically troubled. But Jane’s refusal remains significant. Her own judgement has authority even when desire argues against it. She does not have to become indifferent before she is entitled to go.

Romance need not abandon dangerous characters, impossible longing or extravagant pleasure. It can contain the whole unruly range of desire. What deserves resistance is the bargain that asks a woman to surrender her judgement in exchange for being chosen.

The most radical romantic ending may be one in which being loved leaves a woman fully able to say no—and the story knows she has lost none of her worth.
